title: Logarithmic Hodge Complexes And Smooth Open Weights

items.title: SNC projective compactifications of smooth quasiprojective varieties
items.statement: Assume AC. Every smooth quasiprojective complex variety $U$ admits a smooth projective compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ with reduced boundary a simple normal crossings divisor $D$. Given finitely many such compactifications, there is another dominating all of them and restricting to the identity on $U$. A morphism of smooth quasiprojective varieties extends to a morphism of such compactifications after modifying the source compactification outside its open variety.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; a smooth quasiprojective complex variety $U$, meaning a separated finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme ([[def-separated-morphism-schemes]], [[def-locally-finite-type-and-finite-type-morphism]]) whose structure morphism to $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$ is H-quasi-projective ([[def-quasi-projective-morphism]]); $U$ need not be connected or irreducible, and its finitely many connected components are treated separately. A **compactification** of $U$ is an open immersion $U\hookrightarrow X$ into a proper $\mathbb C$-scheme with dense image ([[def-open-immersion-schemes]]); it is **smooth projective** when $X$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]) and $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$ is H-projective ([[def-projective-morphism-pre-proj]]), and its **boundary** is the complement of the image with its reduced structure. An **SNC compactification** is one whose boundary is a reduced effective Cartier divisor with simple normal crossings support ([[def-simple-normal-crossings-divisors]]), interpreted on each pure-dimensional component when dimensions differ.

[F1] Quasi-projectivity unpacked: the structure morphism $U\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$ factors, for some $n\ge0$, through a quasi-compact immersion $U\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ followed by the projection; an immersion factors as a closed immersion into an open subscheme ([[def-quasi-projective-morphism]], [[def-locally-closed-immersion]], [[def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-morphism]], [[def-closed-immersion-schemes]]).

[F2] Scheme-theoretic image: for a quasi-compact morphism $f:X\to Y$, the kernel $\mathcal K=\ker(\mathcal O_Y\to f_*\mathcal O_X)$ is a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf and $V(\mathcal K)$ is the smallest closed subscheme of $Y$ through which $f$ factors; its restriction to every open $W\subseteq Y$ is the scheme-theoretic image of $f^{-1}(W)\to W$ ([[def-scheme-theoretic-image]], [[thm-scheme-theoretic-image-quasi-compact-morphism]]).

[F3] Weak embedded desingularization: for a field $K$ of characteristic zero, a smooth finite-type $K$-scheme $P$ and a reduced closed subscheme $Y\subseteq P$, there is a sequence $P=P_0\leftarrow P_1\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow P_r$ of blowups of regular centers $C_{i-1}\subseteq P_{i-1}$ such that every center is disjoint from the smooth locus of the strict transform $Y_i$, the strict transform $Y_r$ is smooth and has simple normal crossings with the exceptional divisor, and the induced morphism $Y_r\to Y$ is an isomorphism over the smooth locus of $Y$; the construction is canonical and commutes with smooth morphisms and ambient embeddings ([[thm-weak-embedded-desingularization]]).

[F4] Principalization: for a field $K$ of characteristic zero, a smooth finite-type $K$-scheme $X$ and a coherent ideal sheaf $\mathcal I$ that is not identically zero on any irreducible component of $X$, there is a sequence $X=X_0\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow X_s$ of blowups of regular centers with $\sigma^*\mathcal I$ the ideal of an effective Cartier divisor whose support has simple normal crossings; the centers of the underlying canonical resolution of the marked ideal $(\mathcal I,\varnothing,1)$ lie in its successive supports, and the controlled transform satisfies $\sigma_i^*\mathcal I_{i-1}=\mathcal I(D_i)\cdot\mathcal I_i$, so that $\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal I_i)\subseteq\sigma_i^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\mathcal I)$ ([[thm-principalization-of-ideals]], [[prop-canonical-resolution-of-marked-ideals]], [[def-multiple-test-blowup-and-controlled-transform]], [[def-simple-normal-crossings-divisors]]).

[F5] Projectivity devices: on a scheme projective over a Noetherian ring, twisting a coherent sheaf by a large power of an ample invertible sheaf makes it globally generated ([[lem-eventual-global-generation-coherent-twists]], [[def-ample-invertible-sheaf]]); for an integral finite-type $k$-scheme $X$, an invertible sheaf $L$ and meromorphic sections $s_0,\dots,s_n$ of $L$ not all zero, the blowup $B$ of the fractional ideal $I=(\sum_i\mathcal O_Xs_i)\otimes L^{-1}$ is the schematic closure of the graph of the ratio map and $(\pi,\psi):B\hookrightarrow X\times_k\mathbb P^n_k$ is a closed immersion, with $B=\operatorname{Proj}_X(\bigoplus_{d\ge0}I^d)$ ([[cor-rational-map-to-projective-space-resolved-by-base-ideal-blowup]], [[def-blowup-scheme-along-ideal]]); $\mathbb P^m_S\times_S\mathbb P^n_S\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^{(m+1)(n+1)-1}_S$ is a closed immersion ([[thm-segre-line-bundle-external-tensor]]); the pullback of $\mathcal O(1)$ along a closed immersion is H-very ample, hence ample over an affine base ([[lem-very-ample-implies-ample]]); closed immersions are stable under base change, and a composite of closed immersions is a closed immersion, since a homeomorphism onto a closed subset and a surjection of structure sheaves compose to such ([[lem-base-change-open-closed-immersions]], [[def-closed-immersion-schemes]]).

[F6] Regularity and smoothness: a smooth morphism at a point has geometrically regular scheme-theoretic fibre there, so a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme is regular and reduced, regular local rings being domains ([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]], [[thm-regular-local-rings-are-domains-and-cohen-macaulay]], [[def-regular-local-ring-geometric-point]]); in characteristic zero a finite-type scheme over a field is smooth if and only if all its local rings are regular ([[rem-resolution-of-singularities-conventions]], [[lem-ag-geometric-regularity-field-tests]]); a regular point of a reduced Noetherian scheme lies on exactly one irreducible component ([[lem-regular-point-lies-on-one-component]], [[def-irreducible-component-scheme]]); smoothness is stable under base change and composition ([[thm-smooth-morphisms-stable-base-change-composition]]), and étale is smooth of relative dimension zero ([[def-etale-morphism-schemes]]); étale morphisms are stable under base change and composition ([[lem-etale-stable-base-change-composition]]).

[F7] Regular immersions and blowup charts: for a closed immersion $C\hookrightarrow Y$ of smooth finite-type schemes over a field with pure dimensions and constant codimension, locally in the étale topology the embedding is the inverse image of a coordinate inclusion $\mathbb A^n\subset\mathbb A^m$ ([[lem-smooth-immersion-normal-sequence-and-deformation-charts]]); blowups commute with flat base change along $g$ for the inverse image ideal, $\operatorname{Bl}_{g^{-1}\mathcal I}X'\cong\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X\times_XX'$ ([[thm-blowup-base-change-flat]]); the blowup is an isomorphism off the zero scheme of the ideal ([[lem-blowup-isomorphism-off-center]]); blowups restrict to open subschemes of the base ([[lem-blowup-local-on-base-scheme]]); a blowup of a nonzero finite-type ideal on an integral scheme is integral ([[lem-blowup-reduced-integral-under-domain-rees]]), and is finite type and proper ([[thm-blowup-projective]]); affine blowup charts are $\operatorname{Spec}A[I/a]$ with $IA[I/a]=aA[I/a]$ and $(A[I/a])_a=A_a$ ([[thm-affine-blowup-standard-charts]], [[lem-affine-blowup-algebra-properties]]).

[F8] Finite type versus coherent: on a locally Noetherian scheme a quasi-coherent module of finite type is coherent ([[thm-coherent-sheaves-abelian-noetherian-scheme]], [[def-coherent-module-scheme]], [[def-quasi-coherent-ideal-sheaf]]).

[A1] AC is assumed in the statement and consumed through the suppliers above (scheme-theoretic images, canonical resolution and principalization centers, Serre generation, the graph-closure corollary, Segre and ample-pullback items); the divisor, component and diagonal/graph bookkeeping below is choice-free. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct: reduce the quasiprojective variety to a reduced projective closure, assemble projectivity and smoothness of blowups along regular centers from the published resolution and blowup development, and then desingularize the closure and principalize its boundary ideal.

1.1 Closure of a quasi-compact immersion. Let $f:W\to P$ be a quasi-compact immersion from a reduced finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme into a Noetherian scheme, factored as a closed immersion $W\hookrightarrow V$ followed by an open immersion $V\hookrightarrow P$. By [F2] its scheme-theoretic image $Z=V(\mathcal K)$, $\mathcal K=\ker(\mathcal O_P\to f_*\mathcal O_W)$, restricts on $V$ to $W$, so $W$ is open in $Z$ with the same local rings. On an affine open $T=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq P$, the kernel $\mathcal K(T)$ is radical: if $g^r$ restricts to zero on $f^{-1}(T)$, then $g$ restricts to zero because $W$ is reduced. Thus $A/\mathcal K(T)$ is reduced, proving that $Z$ is reduced. If $W$ were not dense in $Z$, its proper reduced closed closure in $Z$ would receive $f$: its defining sections restrict to functions zero at every point of the reduced scheme $W$, hence zero on every affine open of $W$. This contradicts minimality of the scheme-theoretic image, so $W$ is dense. Every irreducible component meets $W$: the complement of the finitely many other components is a nonempty open subset of $Z$ contained in that component, since an irreducible component cannot be contained in their finite union; density forces this open to meet $W$. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Blowups of integral projective schemes are projective. Let $Y$ be an integral finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme whose structure morphism is H-projective, and let $\mathcal I$ be a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf of finite type. If $\mathcal I=0$ then $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y=\operatorname{Proj}_Y(\mathcal O_Y\oplus0\oplus\cdots)=\varnothing$, which is projective as the empty closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^0_{\mathbb C}$; assume $\mathcal I\ne0$. Fix a closed immersion $Y\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}$ and let $L=\mathcal O_Y(1)$ be the pullback of $\mathcal O(1)$, which is H-very ample by construction and ample over the affine base $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$; $Y$ is Noetherian and $\mathcal I$ is coherent, so for some $m\ge0$ the twist $\mathcal I(m)=\mathcal I\otimes L^{\otimes m}$ is globally generated. Its evaluation map $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal I(m))\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathcal O_Y\to\mathcal I(m)$ is surjective and $Y$ is quasi-compact with $\mathcal I(m)$ of finite type, so finitely many global sections $s_0,\dots,s_n$ already generate $\mathcal I(m)$: on a finite affine cover, a finitely generated module generated by the image of the global sections is generated by finitely many of them. Put $L'=L^{\otimes m}$, view the $s_i$ as meromorphic sections of the invertible sheaf $L'$, and set $F=\sum_i\mathcal O_Ys_i=\mathcal I(m)$ and $I=F\otimes L'^{-1}=\mathcal I$, so the ratio map of the $s_i$ is $Y\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$. The graph-closure corollary gives $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y=\operatorname{Proj}_Y(\bigoplus_{d\ge0}I^d)=B$ with a closed immersion $(\pi,\psi):B\hookrightarrow Y\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$. Composing with the closed immersion $Y\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ obtained by base change of $Y\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}$ and then with the Segre embedding, itself a closed immersion, exhibits $B$ as a closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^{(N+1)(n+1)-1}_{\mathbb C}$; hence the structure morphism of $B$ is H-projective. [F5, F7, F8, construct, algebra]

1.3 Disjoint unions of projective schemes are projective. Let $Z_1,\dots,Z_t\subseteq\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$ be closed subschemes with pairwise disjoint underlying sets and ideals $\mathcal I_\alpha$. The product ideal $\mathcal J=\mathcal I_1\cdots\mathcal I_t$ equals the intersection $\bigcap_\alpha\mathcal I_\alpha$: on an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}A$ the ideals $J_\alpha$ of the $Z_\alpha$ satisfy $V(J_\alpha)\cap V(J_\beta)=\varnothing$ for $\alpha\ne\beta$, so $J_\alpha+J_\beta=A$ and the product of pairwise comaximal ideals is their intersection. At a point $x\in Z_\alpha$ one has $\mathcal I_{\beta,x}=\mathcal O_x$ for $\beta\ne\alpha$, so $\mathcal J_x=\mathcal I_{\alpha,x}$; therefore $V(\mathcal J)=\bigsqcup_\alpha Z_\alpha$ as subschemes of $\mathbb P^M$, and the natural morphism $\bigsqcup_\alpha Z_\alpha\to\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$ is a closed immersion. Now let $X_1,\dots,X_t$ be projective $\mathbb C$-schemes, say $X_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb P^{M_\alpha}_{\mathbb C}$ closed. The coordinate-block maps $\mathbb P^{M_\alpha}_{\mathbb C}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$, $M=\sum_\alpha(M_\alpha+1)-1$, identify the projective spaces with pairwise disjoint linear subspaces (vanishing of all coordinates outside one block), and are closed immersions; the images of the $X_\alpha$ are closed subschemes with pairwise disjoint underlying sets, so the preceding paragraph realizes $\bigsqcup_\alpha X_\alpha$ as a closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$. Hence a finite disjoint union of projective $\mathbb C$-schemes is projective over $\mathbb C$. [F5, given, construct, algebra]

1.4 Local reduction to pure dimensions and constant codimension. Let $Y$ be a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme and $C\subseteq Y$ a regular closed subscheme with ideal sheaf $\mathcal I$, a coherent ideal. Fix $x\in C$; if $C=\varnothing$ there is nothing to prove. Since smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-schemes and regular finite-type $\mathbb C$-schemes are smooth over $\mathbb C$ in characteristic zero, $C$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$ and, being regular Noetherian and reduced, each of its points lies on exactly one irreducible component; the components of $C$ are therefore pairwise disjoint, finitely many, and each is a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme of pure dimension $n$, with local rings equal to those of $C$ at its points. Let $C_0$ be the component through $x$ and let $Y^\circ$ be the connected component of $Y$ containing $x$; it is a single irreducible component, hence pure of dimension $m$, and open in $Y$. Choose an affine open $U\subseteq Y^\circ$ containing $x$ and disjoint from $C\smallsetminus C_0$ (a finite union of closed sets missing $x$). Then $U$ is smooth of pure dimension $m$, $C\cap U=C_0\cap U$ is closed in $U$, smooth, irreducible of dimension $n$, and the closed immersion $C\cap U\hookrightarrow U$ has constant codimension $d=m-n$. [F6, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Regularity and components. A point $w\in W$ is a regular point of $Z$: the local rings of $Z$ and $W$ at $w$ coincide by step 1.1, and a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme has regular local rings. Every irreducible component of $Z$ meets $W$: for a component $Z_\alpha$ of the reduced Noetherian $Z$, the complement of the union of the finitely many other components is a nonempty open subset of $Z$ contained in $Z_\alpha$, nonemptiness holding because otherwise irreducibility of $Z_\alpha$ would place it inside one of the other components, contradicting maximality; and the dense open $W$ meets every nonempty open subset. If $Z$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$, as the schemes $P$, $P_i$ and $Z'$ below are, then its irreducible components are pairwise disjoint: a common point of two components would give the local ring there two distinct minimal primes and hence a non-domain, whereas a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme has regular local rings, which are domains. Consequently, for smooth $Z$, the components are finitely many pairwise disjoint integral closed subschemes, open and closed in $Z$. [F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Blowups preserve finite disjoint unions of integral projective schemes. Let $X=\bigsqcup_\alpha X_\alpha$ with each $X_\alpha$ integral, finite type and H-projective over $\mathbb C$, and let $\mathcal I$ be a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf of finite type on $X$; write $\mathcal I_\alpha=\mathcal I|_{X_\alpha}$. Since the pieces are open and closed, the blowup restricts: $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X\cong\bigsqcup_\alpha\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I_\alpha}X_\alpha$. If $\mathcal I_\alpha=0$ then that piece is empty; if $\mathcal I_\alpha\ne0$ then $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I_\alpha}X_\alpha$ is integral, finite type and H-projective by step 1.2. So the blowup is again a finite disjoint union of integral projective $\mathbb C$-schemes, and it is projective over $\mathbb C$ by step 1.3; the relevant ideals are quasi-coherent of finite type, as ideals of closed subschemes of finite-type $\mathbb C$-schemes (affine-locally the kernel of a surjection of Noetherian rings, hence finitely generated). [F7, F8, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

2.3 Smoothness of the blowup along a regular center. Keep the notation of step 1.4 and first blow up the coordinate subspace: for $A=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_m]$ and $I=(x_{n+1},\dots,x_m)$, the chart of $\operatorname{Bl}_I\operatorname{Spec}A$ indexed by $x_j$ ($n<j\le m$) is $\operatorname{Spec}A[I/x_j]$, and $A[I/x_j]$ is generated over $A$ by the fractions $x_l/x_j$ ($n<l\le m$, $l\ne j$); substituting $x_l=y_lx_j$ exhibits it as the polynomial ring $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n,x_j,\ y_l\ (n<l\le m,\ l\ne j)]$, the two presentations agreeing inside $A_{x_j}$ because the $y_l$ are algebraically independent over $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n,x_j]$ (clearing denominators uses only that $x_j$ is a nonzerodivisor). Hence $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathbb A^n}\mathbb A^m$ is covered by affine spaces and is smooth over $\mathbb C$. Now by [F7] the closed immersion $C\cap U\hookrightarrow U$ of step 1.4 is, at each of its points, locally in the étale topology the inverse image of the coordinate inclusion $\mathbb A^n\subset\mathbb A^m$: there are a Zariski open $V\subseteq U$ and an étale morphism $\varphi:V\to\mathbb A^m_{\mathbb C}$ with $\varphi^{-1}(\mathbb A^n)=C\cap V$ as closed subschemes. Since $\varphi$ is flat and blowups commute with flat base change along the inverse image ideal, $\operatorname{Bl}_{C\cap V}V\cong\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathbb A^n}\mathbb A^m\times_{\mathbb A^m}V$. The projection of this fibre product to $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathbb A^n}\mathbb A^m$ is the base change of the étale morphism $\varphi$, hence étale, and étale morphisms are smooth; a composite of smooth morphisms is smooth, so the model base change, and therefore $\operatorname{Bl}_{C\cap V}V$, is smooth over $\mathbb C$. [F6, F7, step 1.4, construct, algebra]

3.1 Conclusion for one blowup and for sequences. With $\pi:\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y\to Y$ and $x\in C$ as in step 1.4, choose the open $V$ of step 2.3 around $x$; the open subscheme $\pi^{-1}(V)$ of the blowup is smooth over $\mathbb C$. Points of $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y$ mapping outside $C$ lie in the open subscheme $\pi^{-1}(Y\smallsetminus C)$, which is isomorphic to the smooth scheme $Y\smallsetminus C$; as $x$ ranges over $C$, these opens cover $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y$, and smoothness is local on the source, so $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$. The blowup is finite type over $\mathbb C$, so the same statement applies to it in place of $Y$: if $C_1\subseteq Y_1$ is a regular closed subscheme of a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme $Y_1$, then $\operatorname{Bl}_{C_1}Y_1$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$. By induction, every scheme obtained from a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme by a finite sequence of blowups along regular closed subschemes is smooth over $\mathbb C$. [F6, F7, step 1.4, step 2.3, construct]

3.2 The model construction: desingularizing the closure. Let $P$ be a smooth projective $\mathbb C$-scheme, $Z\subseteq P$ a reduced closed subscheme and $W\subseteq Z$ an open dense subscheme that is smooth over $\mathbb C$. Apply [F3] to $Z\subseteq P$: there is a sequence $P=P_0\leftarrow P_1\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow P_r$ of blowups of regular centers with strict transforms $Z_i\subseteq P_i$, and $Z'=Z_r$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$ with the composite $P_r\to P$ an isomorphism over the smooth locus of $Z$, hence over $W$. Each $P_i$ is a finite disjoint union of integral projective $\mathbb C$-schemes: $P_0=P$ is smooth projective, so it is such a union by step 2.1, and each step is a blowup along the ideal sheaf of a regular closed subscheme, a coherent ideal, so step 2.2 applies inductively. Let $W'$ be the preimage of $W$ in $Z'$; it is open in $Z'$ and isomorphic to $W$. Every irreducible component of $Z'$ meets $W'$: the composite $Z'\to Z$ is proper and birational on every component, so a component of $Z'$ maps onto a component of $Z$; a component of $Z'$ disjoint from $W'$ would have image contained in $Z\smallsetminus W$, a closed set, but every component of $Z$ meets the dense open $W$ by step 2.1, a contradiction. Consequently the ideal $\mathcal I\subseteq\mathcal O_{Z'}$ of the reduced closed subscheme $Z'\smallsetminus W'$ is coherent and is not identically zero on any irreducible component of $Z'$. [F3, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 The model construction: principalizing the boundary. Keep step 3.2 and decompose $Z'=\bigsqcup_\alpha Z'_\alpha$ into its finitely many components, open and closed in $Z'$ by step 2.1. For each $\alpha$, apply [F4] to the smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme $Z'_\alpha$ and the restricted ideal $\mathcal I_\alpha$ if $\mathcal I_\alpha\ne\mathcal O_{Z'_\alpha}$, and take the identity sequence if $\mathcal I_\alpha=\mathcal O_{Z'_\alpha}$; the centers lie in the successive supports, which map into $\operatorname{supp}\mathcal I_\alpha$, so at every step the blowup is an isomorphism over the complement of the preimage of $\operatorname{supp}\mathcal I_\alpha$, and the composite $\sigma_\alpha:X_\alpha\to Z'_\alpha$ is an isomorphism over $Z'_\alpha\smallsetminus\operatorname{supp}\mathcal I_\alpha$. Set $X=\bigsqcup_\alpha X_\alpha$ and $\sigma=\bigsqcup_\alpha\sigma_\alpha$. Each $X_\alpha$ is a finite sequence of blowups of the integral projective scheme $Z'_\alpha$ along regular centers: by step 2.2 each intermediate scheme is a finite disjoint union of integral projective $\mathbb C$-schemes, and by step 3.1 it is smooth; hence each $X_\alpha$ is integral (or empty), smooth and projective, and $X$ is smooth and projective by step 1.3. On each $Z'_\alpha$ with $\mathcal I_\alpha\ne\mathcal O_{Z'_\alpha}$, the total transform $\sigma_\alpha^*\mathcal I_\alpha$ is the ideal of an effective Cartier divisor with SNC support; on pieces with $\mathcal I_\alpha=\mathcal O_{Z'_\alpha}$ it is the unit ideal, defining the zero divisor with empty support. Let $D\subseteq X$ be the union of these supports with reduced structure: its ideal is, locally, generated by the products of the components' equations, so $D$ is a reduced effective Cartier divisor with simple normal crossings support. Finally $\sigma$ is an isomorphism over $Z'\smallsetminus\operatorname{supp}\mathcal I=W'$, so $X\smallsetminus D\cong W'\cong W$, and the composite morphism $c:X\to P_r\to\cdots\to P$ restricts to the given open immersion $W\hookrightarrow Z\subseteq P$. This proves: (C) for every smooth projective $P$, reduced closed $Z\subseteq P$ and open dense smooth $W\subseteq Z$, there are a smooth projective $X$, a reduced SNC divisor $D\subseteq X$, an isomorphism $X\smallsetminus D\cong W$ and a morphism $c:X\to P$ inducing the inclusion of $W$; moreover $X$ is a finite disjoint union of integral projective pieces. [F4, F6, F7, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 Existence of an SNC projective compactification. By [F1] there is a quasi-compact immersion $\iota:U\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$; let $Z\subseteq\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ be its scheme-theoretic image, so that $U\cong Z\cap V$ is open and dense in the reduced closed subscheme $Z$, with $U$ contained in the regular locus, by steps 1.1 and 2.1. Apply (C) of step 4.1 with $P=\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ and $W=U$: the output $X$ is a finite disjoint union of integral projective smooth $\mathbb C$-schemes with a reduced SNC boundary divisor $D$ and $X\smallsetminus D\cong U$. The exceptional boundary divisor misses the generic point of every component, so its intersection with each irreducible component is a proper closed subset and hence nowhere dense; therefore $X\smallsetminus D$ is dense in $X$, and $j:U\cong X\smallsetminus D\hookrightarrow X$ is a smooth projective compactification with reduced SNC boundary. If $U=\varnothing$ the same construction with $Z=\varnothing$ returns $X=\varnothing$ and the empty divisor, and all claims are vacuous. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 4.1, given, construct]

6.1 Common domination. Let $U\hookrightarrow X_1,\dots,U\hookrightarrow X_t$ be smooth projective compactifications, and put $P=X_1\times_{\mathbb C}\cdots\times_{\mathbb C}X_t$. Each $X_i$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$ and H-projective, so $P$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$ by stability of smoothness under base change and composition, and projective over $\mathbb C$: the product of closed immersions $X_1\times_{\mathbb C}\cdots\times_{\mathbb C}X_t\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^{N_1}_{\mathbb C}\times_{\mathbb C}\cdots\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^{N_t}_{\mathbb C}$ is a closed immersion by iterated base change, and the iterated Segre embeddings are closed immersions. The diagonal morphism $\delta:U\to P$ is an immersion: it is the composite of the diagonal $U\to U\times_{\mathbb C}\cdots\times_{\mathbb C}U$, a closed immersion because $U$ is separated over $\mathbb C$, with the product of the open immersions $U\hookrightarrow X_i$, which is an open immersion; it is quasi-compact because $U$ is Noetherian and $P$ is quasi-compact. Let $Z$ be its scheme-theoretic image; by step 1.1, $Z$ is reduced with $W:=\delta(U)\cong U$ open, dense and contained in its regular locus. Apply (C) of step 4.1 to $(P,Z,W)$ and compose the resulting morphism $c:X\to P$ with the projections: the composites $X\to X_i$ restrict to the identity of $U$ under the identifications $X\smallsetminus D\cong U$, and $X$ is a smooth projective compactification of $U$ with reduced SNC boundary dominating all $X_i$. For the empty family, step 5.1 already supplies a compactification. [F1, F2, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Extension of morphisms. Let $\varphi:U\to V$ be a morphism of smooth quasiprojective complex varieties and let $U\hookrightarrow\tilde U$, $V\hookrightarrow\tilde V$ be smooth projective compactifications. Set $P=\tilde U\times_{\mathbb C}\tilde V$; as in step 6.1 it is smooth and projective. Consider the morphism $\gamma=(\iota,\varphi):U\to P$, where $\iota$ is the open immersion $U\hookrightarrow\tilde U$; it factors as the graph morphism $U\to U\times_{\mathbb C}V$, a closed immersion because $V$ is separated over $\mathbb C$, followed by the open immersion $U\times_{\mathbb C}V\hookrightarrow\tilde U\times_{\mathbb C}\tilde V$, so $\gamma$ is an immersion, and it is quasi-compact because $U$ is Noetherian. Let $Z$ be the scheme-theoretic image of $\gamma$; by step 1.1, $Z$ is reduced and $W:=\gamma(U)\cong U$ is open, dense and smooth inside $Z$. Apply (C) of step 4.1 to $(P,Z,W)$, obtaining a smooth projective compactification $X$ of $U$ with reduced SNC boundary and a morphism $c:X\to P$ inducing $\gamma$ on $U$. Then the composite of $c$ with the second projection $P\to\tilde V$ is a morphism $X\to\tilde V$ restricting to $\varphi$ on $U$, and the composite with the first projection is a morphism $X\to\tilde U$ restricting to the identity on $U$; so $\varphi$ extends after modifying the source compactification outside $U$. Two extensions obtained from the same data coincide on $U$, and the construction of step 6.1 applied to the two source modifications makes the resulting pullback maps agree on $U$. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, construct]

8.1 Choice accounting and boundaries. AC is assumed in the statement and is consumed exactly through the suppliers of [F1]--[F8]: the scheme-theoretic image theorem and the quasi-coherent ideal correspondence, the weak embedded desingularization and principalization algorithms with their canonical regular centers and finite blowup sequences, the Serre-generation theorem behind global generation, the graph-closure corollary and the Segre and ample-pullback items, the étale-local model of regular immersions together with flat base change of blowups, and the coherence identification; all of these either assume AC directly or inherit it from the relative Proj and blowup constructions. The construction uses no further selection: components, divisors and morphisms are constructed canonically or transported along given maps, and the finite disjoint unions, diagonal and graph arguments are choice-free. [A1, step 1.3, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1] ∎

items.title: Modification preserves open cohomology images
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $p:X'\to X$ be a proper morphism between smooth projective complex varieties of equal pure dimension, restricting to the identity on a common open variety $U$. Then $H^n(X,\mathbb Q)$ and $H^n(X',\mathbb Q)$ have the same image in $H^n(U,\mathbb Q)$ for every $n$. Consequently the compactification-image formula of logarithmic weights extends from an SNC compactification to every smooth projective compactification.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; a smooth quasiprojective complex variety $U$; smooth projective complex varieties $X,X'$ of the same pure dimension $d$; open immersions $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ and $j':U\hookrightarrow X'$ whose images need not be dense for the first sentence (step 1.1 reduces to the dense case) ([[def-open-immersion-schemes]]); a morphism $p:X'\to X$ with $p\circ j'=j$. Below $H^*(-;\mathbb Q)$ denotes singular cohomology of the analytic spaces of [F1, F2], and all maps between them are the induced continuous maps of [F1, F3].

[F1] Analytification and orientation ([[lem-smooth-projective-analytification-has-rational-kahler-polarization]], [[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). A smooth projective complex variety of pure dimension $d$ has an analytification that is a compact Hausdorff second-countable complex manifold of complex dimension $d$, a finite discrete set when $d=0$; every standard smooth algebraic chart becomes a holomorphic chart and every morphism of smooth complex varieties induces a holomorphic, hence continuous, map. A complex manifold carries the canonical orientation for which $(v_1,Jv_1,\dots,v_d,Jv_d)$ is positive on a complex basis, and it is boundaryless; an ample class is represented by a positive closed real $(1,1)$-form, so $X$ and $X'$ are compact Kaehler, hence compact oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifolds, and every open subvariety is an oriented complex submanifold. The analytic topology of a complex algebraic variety is the one of the cited definition, and regular maps are continuous for it.

[F2] Poincare duality ([[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds]], [[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]]). For the oriented boundaryless manifolds $X,X'$ of real dimension $2d$ and $U$, cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms $D_M:H_c^p(M;\mathbb Q)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{2d-p}(M;\mathbb Q)$ for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;\mathbb Q)=H^p(M;\mathbb Q)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$, where $[M]$ is the fundamental class of the cited definition. For the open inclusions $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ and $j':U\hookrightarrow X'$ with restricted orientation, $D_X(e_Xc)=j_*D_Uc$ and $D_{X'}(e_{X'}c)=j'_*D_Uc$ for every $c\in H_c^p(U;\mathbb Q)$, where $e_X,e_{X'}$ are extension of compact supports.

[F3] Kronecker pairing ([[def-kronecker-evaluation-pairing]], [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]], [[cor-cohomology-over-a-field-is-dual-to-homology-over-that-field]], [[prop-singular-cohomology-is-contravariantly-functorial]], [[prop-singular-chains-and-homology-are-covariantly-functorial]]). For every space $M$ and integer $n$, evaluation $\Phi:H^n(M;\mathbb Q)\times H_n(M;\mathbb Q)\to\mathbb Q$, $\Phi(\alpha,z)=\langle\alpha,z\rangle$, is $\mathbb Q$-bilinear, independent of cocycle and cycle representatives, natural, $\Phi(f^*\alpha,z)=\Phi(\alpha,f_*z)$ for continuous $f$, and over the field $\mathbb Q$ the map $\alpha\mapsto\Phi(\alpha,-)$ is an isomorphism onto the full linear dual of $H_n(M;\mathbb Q)$; pullback and pushforward are functorial, $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$ and $(g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*$.

[F4] Cap product and cup product ([[def-cap-product-with-cohomology-first]], [[thm-cap-product-boundary-identity]], [[prop-cap-product-naturality-and-projection-formula]]). Cap evaluates the front face and retains the back face with no additional sign, is well defined on (co)homology classes, and in degree $n$ on an $n$-cycle it returns $\varphi(\sigma)$ times the last vertex. For continuous $f$ and classes for which the expressions are defined, $f_*(f^*\alpha\cap x)=\alpha\cap f_*x$ and $(\alpha\smile\beta)\cap x=\beta\cap(\alpha\cap x)$.

[F5] Augmentation ([[def-zero-simplex-augmentation-and-reduced-singular-homology]], [[lem-singular-augmentation-commutes-with-boundary]]). The augmentation $\varepsilon_M:C_0(M;\mathbb Q)\to\mathbb Q$ sends every singular $0$-simplex generator to $1$; it kills $1$-boundaries, so it descends to $\varepsilon_*:H_0(M;\mathbb Q)\to\mathbb Q$.

[F6] Graded commutativity ([[thm-singular-cohomology-is-graded-commutative]]). For $a\in H^p(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $b\in H^q(M;\mathbb Q)$, $a\smile b=(-1)^{pq}b\smile a$.

[F7] Compact supports and excision ([[def-compactly-supported-singular-cohomology-of-a-locally-compact-space]], [[thm-excision-for-singular-cohomology]]). $H_c^p(X;\mathbb Q)$ is the colimit of the groups $H^p(X,X\setminus K;\mathbb Q)$ over compact $K\subseteq X$, with transition maps induced by inclusion of relative cochain complexes; $X$ and $X'$ are compact Hausdorff, so $X\setminus K$ is open for compact $K$. If $K\subseteq U$ is compact, then $\overline{X\setminus U}=X\setminus U\subseteq X\setminus K=\operatorname{int}_X(X\setminus K)$ and similarly in $X'$, so excision identifies $j^*:H^p(X,X\setminus K;\mathbb Q)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^p(U,U\setminus K;\mathbb Q)$ and $(j')^*:H^p(X',X'\setminus K;\mathbb Q)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^p(U,U\setminus K;\mathbb Q)$. The extension maps $e_X:H_c^p(U;\mathbb Q)\to H_c^p(X;\mathbb Q)$ and $e_{X'}:H_c^p(U;\mathbb Q)\to H_c^p(X';\mathbb Q)$ are the colimit maps induced by $(j^*)^{-1}$ and $((j')^*)^{-1}$ at each support $K\subseteq U$; these systems are compatible with the transition maps because the same restriction maps compute both sides.

[F8] Compactification and domination ([[lem-smooth-quasiprojective-varieties-admit-snc-projective-compactifications]]). $U$ admits a smooth projective compactification with reduced SNC boundary; and a morphism of smooth quasiprojective varieties extends to a morphism of smooth projective compactifications after modifying the source compactification outside its open variety, the modified source and the target being arbitrary smooth projective compactifications as recorded in the closing remark of that lemma.

[F9] Smooth schemes over $\mathbb C$ are reduced, with regular local rings that are domains ([[thm-regular-local-rings-are-domains-and-cohen-macaulay]]). A separated scheme has closed diagonal ([[def-separated-morphism-schemes]]), so the equalizer of two maps to it is a closed subscheme, whose ideal restricts to zero wherever the maps agree ([[def-closed-immersion-schemes]]). On a reduced Noetherian scheme a regular function zero on a dense open is zero: affine-locally it maps to zero in the fraction field of each irreducible component, hence belongs to every minimal prime, whose intersection is the zero nilradical.

[A1] AC is assumed in the statement. It is consumed through [F1] (analytification, Chern-form and comparison suppliers), [F2] (orientation classes and exhaustions), [F3] (the full dual and bases), [F7] (the compact-support colimit and excision) and [F8] (resolution, principalization and Serre generation), and through [F9] (regular local domains). The separatedness and reducedness argument, and the cap, cup, sequence and pairing computations below, are otherwise choice-free. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct: realize both compactifications as compact oriented manifolds, compare the two restriction maps through Poincare duality and the cap-cup compatibility, and finish with the domination clause of [F8].

1.1 Structure of the spaces. For the first sentence, discard the open-and-closed components of $X$ and $X'$ that do not meet $U$. Smooth projective components are integral by the regular-local-domain argument [F9], so the remaining open $U$ is dense in each. On each retained component of $X'$, its dense part in $U$ maps to one component of $X$; continuity makes the entire component map into that closed target component. Thus $p$ restricts to the retained unions. Singular chains split over these finitely many open-and-closed components, so discarding the others does not change either restriction image in $H^n(U)$. We may therefore assume the embeddings dense. By [F1], $X$ and $X'$ are compact oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifolds, $U$ is an oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifold, and $j,j'$ are orientation-preserving open embeddings; $p$ is continuous with $p\circ j'=j$. The cohomology groups and maps below are those of these analytic spaces. When $d=0$ the spaces are finite discrete, the dense open embeddings are bijective, and the assertions hold by inspection. [F1, F9, given, algebra]

1.2 The morphism is the identity over $U$. Put $V=p^{-1}(j(U))$, an algebraic open subset of $X'$ containing the dense open $j'(U)$. The maps $V\to X'$ given by inclusion and $j'\circ j^{-1}\circ p$ agree on $j'(U)$. Their equalizer is a closed subscheme by separatedness, and its defining sections vanish on the dense open $j'(U)$; reducedness and [F9] make those sections zero. Thus the two maps agree on all of $V$, and every point of $V$ belongs to $j'(U)$. Hence $p^{-1}(j(U))=j'(U)$ and $p$ restricts there to $j\circ(j')^{-1}$. In particular, for every compact $K\subseteq U$, $p^{-1}(j(K))=j'(K)$ on the analytic spaces. [F9, given, construct, algebra]

1.3 The augmentation evaluates the Kronecker pairing through cap. For every space $M$, $\alpha\in H^n(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $z\in H_n(M;\mathbb Q)$ one has $\Phi(\alpha,z)=\varepsilon_*([\alpha\cap z])$. Choose a cocycle $\varphi$ and a cycle $z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\sigma$ representing the two classes; the defining cap formula in degree $n$ gives $\varphi\cap z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)[\sigma(n)]$, a finite sum of last-vertex generators, and $\varepsilon_*$ of its class is $\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)=\Phi(\alpha,z)$. Both sides are well defined on classes: cap descends by [F4] and $\varepsilon$ descends by [F5]. [F3, F4, F5, algebra]

1.4 The pairings. For $M=X$ or $X'$ define $\Lambda_M(\alpha,\beta):=\Phi(\alpha,D_M\beta)$ for $\alpha\in H^n(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $\beta\in H^{2d-n}(M;\mathbb Q)$, and define $\Lambda_U(\alpha,c):=\Phi(\alpha,D_Uc)$ for $\alpha\in H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ and $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$. Each $\Lambda$ is $\mathbb Q$-bilinear and perfect: $D_M$ and $D_U$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so for $\alpha\ne0$ there is $z$ with $\Phi(\alpha,z)\ne0$ and $z=D\beta$ for a unique $\beta$, whence $\Lambda(\alpha,\beta)\ne0$; conversely, if $\beta\ne0$ then $D\beta\ne0$ and evaluation at the nonzero class $D\beta$ is a nonzero functional on the full dual of homology, realized by some $\alpha$ because $\Phi$ identifies cohomology with that full dual by [F3]. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Cap, cup and the fundamental class. For a closed oriented $2d$-manifold $M$, $\alpha\in H^n(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $\beta\in H^{2d-n}(M;\mathbb Q)$, one has $\Phi(\beta,D_M\alpha)=\langle\alpha\smile\beta,[M]\rangle$, where the right side abbreviates $\Phi(\alpha\smile\beta,[M])$ for the top-degree Kronecker pairing. Indeed $D_M\alpha=\alpha\cap[M]$ by [F2], and the second cap identity of [F4] gives $(\alpha\smile\beta)\cap[M]=\beta\cap(\alpha\cap[M])=\beta\cap D_M\alpha$; applying $\varepsilon_*$ and step 1.3 in degrees $2d-n$ and $2d$ gives the stated equality. [F2, F4, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 Compatibility of the pairings with the open inclusion. For $\theta\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$ or $\theta\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$ and $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$, one has $\Lambda_U(j^*\theta,c)=\Lambda_X(\theta,e_Xc)$ and $\Lambda_U((j')^*\theta,c)=\Lambda_{X'}(\theta,e_{X'}c)$. Indeed $\Lambda_U(j^*\theta,c)=\Phi(j^*\theta,D_Uc)=\Phi(\theta,j_*D_Uc)=\Phi(\theta,D_X(e_Xc))=\Lambda_X(\theta,e_Xc)$ by the naturality in [F3] and the duality naturality in [F2], and the primed identity is identical. [F2, F3, step 1.4]

2.3 The identity over compact supports. For every $n$ and every $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$ one has $p^*(e_Xc)=e_{X'}c$ in $H_c^{2d-n}(X';\mathbb Q)$, where $p^*$ acts on the relative groups, possible by step 1.2. Choose by [F7] a compact $K\subseteq U$ and $c_K\in H^{2d-n}(U,U\setminus K;\mathbb Q)$ representing $c$; the extension maps send $c$ to the colimit classes represented by $(j^*)^{-1}c_K$ and $((j')^*)^{-1}c_K$. By step 1.2, $p^{-1}(K)=K$, so $p$ induces a map of pairs $(X',X'\setminus K)\to(X,X\setminus K)$ and $p^*$ is defined on these relative groups. Functoriality of pullback gives $(j')^*\circ p^*=(p\circ j')^*=j^*$, so $(j')^*(p^*((j^*)^{-1}c_K))=j^*(j^*)^{-1}c_K=c_K=(j')^*((j')^*)^{-1}c_K$, and injectivity of the excision isomorphism $(j')^*$ gives $p^*((j^*)^{-1}c_K)=((j')^*)^{-1}c_K$; the two colimit classes therefore coincide. [F3, F7, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The transfer and its adjointness. For each $n$ let $T_n:=D_X^{-1}\circ p_*\circ D_{X'}:H^n(X';\mathbb Q)\to H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$, a composite of the duality isomorphisms and the pushforward of [F2] and [F3]. Then, for all $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$ and $b\in H^{2d-n}(X;\mathbb Q)$, one has $\Lambda_X(T_na,b)=\Lambda_{X'}(a,p^*b)$. Write $\sigma=n(2d-n)$. Using step 2.1 and the definition of $T_n$, $\Lambda_X(T_na,b)=\Phi(T_na,D_Xb)=\langle b\smile T_na,[X]\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\langle T_na\smile b,[X]\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\Phi(b,D_XT_na)=(-1)^\sigma\Phi(b,p_*D_{X'}a)$, where the third equality is [F6] and the last is the defining property $D_X\circ T_n=p_*\circ D_{X'}$; naturality from [F3] turns the last term into $(-1)^\sigma\Phi(p^*b,D_{X'}a)$. On the other side, $\Lambda_{X'}(a,p^*b)=\Phi(a,D_{X'}p^*b)=\langle p^*b\smile a,[X']\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\langle a\smile p^*b,[X']\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\Phi(p^*b,D_{X'}a)$ by step 2.1 and [F6]. The two displayed values agree. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The identity on $U$. For every $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$ one has $j^*(T_na)=(j')^*(a)$ in $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$. By perfectness of $\Lambda_U$ in its first variable (step 1.4), it suffices to test against every $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$: $\Lambda_U(j^*(T_na),c)=\Lambda_X(T_na,e_Xc)=\Lambda_{X'}(a,p^*(e_Xc))=\Lambda_{X'}(a,e_{X'}c)=\Lambda_U((j')^*a,c)$, where the first and last equalities are step 2.2, the second is step 3.1 and the third is step 2.3. [step 1.4, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Equality of the images. Let $b\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$. Then $(j')^*(p^*b)=(p\circ j')^*b=j^*b$, by functoriality of pullback [F1, F3], so the image of $H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$ in $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ is contained in the image of $H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$. Conversely, if $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$, step 4.1 exhibits $(j')^*a=j^*(T_na)$ with $T_na\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$, so the reverse inclusion holds and the two images agree for every $n$ with $0\le n\le 2d$. For $n<0$ or $n>2d$ both cohomology groups vanish by duality [F2] and the vanishing conventions of [F3], so both images are $\{0\}$; if $U=\varnothing$ then $X=X'=\varnothing$ because $U$ has dense image, and all groups vanish. This proves the first sentence of the statement. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, step 4.1, given]

6.1 Independence of arbitrary smooth projective compactifications. Let $X$ be an arbitrary smooth projective compactification of $U$, with no SNC hypothesis on its boundary, and let $Z$ be one with reduced SNC boundary, which exists by the first clause of [F8]. Apply the extension clause of [F8] to the identity morphism $U\to U$, viewed with source compactification $Z$ and target compactification $X$: by the closing remark of [F8] the clause is available for arbitrary smooth projective compactifications of the open variety, and it yields a smooth projective compactification $Y$ of $U$ with reduced SNC boundary together with morphisms $Y\to Z$ and $Y\to X$ restricting to the identity on $U$. Since $Y$ is projective and $X$ and $Z$ are separated, the morphisms $Y\to X$ and $Y\to Z$ are proper by [[lem-proper-source-to-separated-target-proper]], and the constructions preserve the component dimensions. Apply step 5.1 on each equal-dimensional component (and take the finite direct sums if dimensions differ); this gives, for every $n$, $\operatorname{im}(H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))=\operatorname{im}(H^n(Y;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))=\operatorname{im}(H^n(Z;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))$. Hence the image subgroup attached to a smooth projective compactification of $U$ is independent of the compactification and may always be computed from one with SNC boundary: any identity expressing that subgroup for an SNC compactification, in particular the compactification-image formula of logarithmic weights, holds for every smooth projective compactification. This proves the second sentence of the statement. [F8, step 5.1, given]

7.1 Choice accounting and boundary cases. AC is assumed in the statement and is consumed exactly through the suppliers of [F1]--[F9]: the analytification with its Chern-form, Jacobian-criterion, ample-power and comparison inputs, Poincare duality with its orientation classes and exhaustions, the full-dual universal coefficient statement, the compact-support colimit and excision, the resolution, principalization and Serre-generation inputs of [F8], and the regular-local-domain supplier of [F9]; all cap, cup, pairing and sequence computations are choice-free. Boundary cases: for $d=0$ all spaces are finite discrete, the groups vanish above degree $0$, $H^0$ has dimension the number of points, $p$ is bijective over $U$ and both images agree; for $U=\varnothing$ all groups vanish; for $n$ outside $0,\ldots,2d$ both groups vanish; for $p=\operatorname{id}_X$ the transfer $T_n$ is the identity; disconnected $X,X',U$ are covered because [F2] and [F3] decompose along components and all formulas are componentwise; the compact support $K$ of step 2.3 may be enlarged and the class $c=0$ or empty $K$ give zero in the same way. Properness of $p$ is stated but not used beyond continuity and $p\circ j'=j$, both of which hold for any morphism of compactifications; no Hodge theory, strictness or mixed structure is used, and no identification of infinite-dimensional vector spaces with double duals is made. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.3, step 5.1, step 6.1, given] ∎

items.title: Logarithmic construction of smooth-open mixed Hodge structures
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $U$ be smooth quasiprojective over $\mathbb C$, and choose an SNC smooth projective compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X$, boundary $D$. The logarithmic de Rham complex with Hodge filtration by degree and pole-count weight filtration constructs a functorial rational mixed Hodge structure on $H^n(U,\mathbb Q)$, independent of the compactification. Its weights are at least $n$, and
$$W_nH^n(U,\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(X,\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H^n(U,\mathbb Q)).$$
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; a smooth quasiprojective complex variety $U$ of pure dimension $d$; an SNC smooth projective compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ with reduced boundary $D$ a simple normal crossings divisor ([[def-simple-normal-crossings-divisors]], [[lem-smooth-quasiprojective-varieties-admit-snc-projective-compactifications]]); the irreducible components $D_1,\dots,D_r$ of $D$ and, for $a\ge0$, the smooth projective scheme $D^{[a]}$ equal to $X$ for $a=0$ and to the disjoint union of the $a$-fold intersections $D_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap D_{i_a}$ for $a\ge1$, with its natural map $i_a:D^{[a]}\to X$ (each summand maps by a closed immersion; the disjoint union need not embed in $X$). Cohomology is singular cohomology of the analytic spaces on the analytic topology of [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]].

[F1] Analytification ([[lem-smooth-projective-analytification-has-rational-kahler-polarization]], [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]], [[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]). $X$ is a compact complex manifold of dimension $d$ with a canonical orientation, $D$ is a reduced divisor with normal crossings, and near every point of $D$ there are holomorphic coordinates $z_1,\dots,z_d$ in which $D$ is $\{z_1\cdots z_s=0\}$ for some $s=s(p)$; each $D^{[a]}$ is a smooth projective complex variety of pure dimension $d-a$ (empty for $a>r$), a morphism of complex varieties induces a holomorphic map, and $U=X\setminus D$ is an open complex submanifold of dimension $d$. Complex-valued smooth forms, the bidegree decomposition, $d=\partial+\bar\partial$ and type are those of [[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]], and holomorphic functions on polydiscs are those of [[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]].

[F2] The de Rham comparison ([[thm-de-rham-theorem]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, integration of smooth forms on smooth simplices is a natural isomorphism $H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\cong H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$ under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, which AC supplies. It applies to the real manifolds underlying $X$, the strata $D^{[a]}$ and $U$, and is compatible with the coefficient extension to $\mathbb C$.

[F3] Hodge theory of the compact strata ([[thm-compact-kahler-hodge-decomposition-via-elliptic-harmonic-forms]], [[lem-smooth-projective-analytification-has-rational-kahler-polarization]], [[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]). Let $V$ be a smooth projective complex variety of pure dimension $m$. Then $H^k(V;\mathbb Q)$ carries a functorial rational pure Hodge structure of weight $k$, whose Hodge filtration is the filtration induced by the holomorphic-degree filtration $\Omega^{\ge p}_V$ of the holomorphic de Rham complex; there is a Hodge decomposition $H^k(V;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(V)$ with $H^{p,q}(V)\cong H^q(V,\Omega^p_V)$; the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence degenerates at $E_1$; and pullback along a morphism and cup product preserve type. In particular $H^k(V;\mathbb Q)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q$.

[F4] Local analytic inputs ([[thm-dolbeault-lemma-polydisc]], [[thm-cohomological-kunneth-isomorphism-under-finite-free-hypotheses]], [[cor-homology-of-spheres]], [[cor-cohomology-over-a-field-is-dual-to-homology-over-that-field]], [[lem-locally-contractible-metric-spaces-have-singular-constant-sheaf-cohomology]]). On a polydisc $P\subseteq\mathbb C^m$, every $\bar\partial$-closed smooth $(p,q)$-form with $q\ge1$ is $\bar\partial$-exact on every smaller relatively compact polydisc. Holomorphic coefficients are continuous and separately holomorphic ([[prop-holomorphic-functions-are-continuous-and-separately-holomorphic]]), admit absolutely normally convergent power series on smaller polydiscs ([[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]]), and these series can be differentiated termwise there ([[thm-power-series-define-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables]]). For a product of circles the Kunneth theorem computes the cohomology as the exterior algebra on the degree-one generators, with each factor contributing one generator because the homology of the circle is $\mathbb Q$ in degrees $0$ and $1$; over the field $\mathbb Q$ the Kronecker evaluation identifies a cohomology group with the full dual of homology, so the classes are detected by their values on the torus cycles.

[F5] Mixed Hodge machinery ([[def-rational-mixed-hodge-structure]], [[def-cohomological-mixed-hodge-complex]], [[lem-mixed-hodge-complexes-give-functorial-cohomology-and-simplicial-weights]], [[lem-morphisms-of-mixed-hodge-structures-are-strict]]). A rational mixed Hodge structure is a $\mathbb Q$-vector space with a finite increasing weight filtration $W$ and a finite decreasing Hodge filtration $F$ on the complexification, opposed on every weight-graded piece; a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex is a filtered pair $(K_{\mathbb Q},(K_{\mathbb C},W))$ with a comparison whose graded pieces are quasi-isomorphisms and whose weight-graded complexes have finite-dimensional cohomology with strict differentials and pure Hodge cohomology of weight $r+w$; a morphism of such complexes induces morphisms of the resulting structures; morphisms of mixed Hodge structures are strict for $W$ and $F$, and the image of a morphism is both a sub- and a quotient structure.

[F6] Sheaves and derived global sections ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]], [[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]], [[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]], [[lem-locally-contractible-metric-spaces-have-singular-constant-sheaf-cohomology]]). Sheaf cohomology is the right derived global-sections functor computed from a supplied functorial injective resolution datum, independent of the datum up to natural isomorphism; for a bounded-below complex of sheaves the same construction is applied to a filtered injective resolution and computes the hypercohomology. On a metric space with a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets, constant-sheaf cohomology agrees with singular cohomology on every open subset.

[F7] Compactification and modification ([[lem-smooth-quasiprojective-varieties-admit-snc-projective-compactifications]], [[lem-smooth-projective-modification-preserves-open-cohomology-images]]). Any finite family of smooth projective compactifications of $U$ is dominated by a smooth projective compactification with reduced SNC boundary restricting to the identity over $U$; a proper morphism of smooth projective varieties of equal pure dimension that is the identity over $U$ does not change the image of $H^n(-;\mathbb Q)$ in $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$.

[F8] Coordinate and divisor inputs. A holomorphic map with invertible complex Jacobian is a local biholomorphism ([[thm-holomorphic-inverse-function-theorem-several-variables]]). Every regular local ring is a UFD ([[thm-nonaffine-regular-local-ring-is-ufd]]), so a nonzero regular germ on smooth $X$ whose zero set is contained in the SNC boundary factors as a unit times powers of its local boundary equations: each irreducible factor is prime; containment of its zero set in the union of the coordinate divisors implies it divides their product, hence one of those equations.

[A1] AC is assumed in the statement and is consumed through [F1] (analytification and orientation), [F2] (the de Rham comparison and its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), [F3] (the compact Kaehler machine), [F4] (the polydisc Dolbeault transform), [F6] (injective resolution data) and [F7] (resolution, principalization and the duality comparison of the modification lemma). AC is also inherited through the local-factoriality supplier of [F8]. The residue, power-series and filtration bookkeeping below is otherwise choice-free. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 (Compactification and strata.) By [F7] choose the SNC smooth projective compactification; the constructions below apply separately to its finitely many smooth connected components when dimensions differ. At a closed point of $X$, the SNC equations are a subset of a regular system of parameters; their differentials extend to a cotangent basis in a smooth chart. The parameter map has invertible complex Jacobian, so [F8] makes these parameters holomorphic coordinates, giving the coordinate divisor model of [F1]. Order the finitely many boundary components to fix residue signs. Their $a$-fold intersections and disjoint unions $D^{[a]}$ are smooth projective by [F1], so [F3] applies to each component. Empty strata contribute zero. [F1, F3, F7, F8, given, construct]

1.2 (Logarithmic forms and the pole filtration.) Put $e_i=dz_i/z_i$ for the $s$ local boundary coordinates. The logarithmic complex $L=\Omega_X^\bullet(\log D)$ is locally generated by $e_1,\ldots,e_s,dz_{s+1},\ldots,dz_d$ over holomorphic functions; regular normal differentials are included because $dz_i=z_ie_i$. Define in degree $k$ the pole-count filtration by $W_aL^k=\sum_{|I|\le a}e_I\wedge\Omega_X^{k-|I|}$, with arbitrary regular holomorphic forms in the second factor, not merely tangential forms. Thus $W_0L=\Omega_X^\bullet$, $W_aL=0$ for $a<0$, and $W_dL=L$. Changing a boundary equation by a unit adds a regular $d\log u$, so this definition is intrinsic. Since $de_i=0$ and differentiating a regular coefficient produces a regular form, $d$ preserves $W$. The degree filtration $F^pL=\Omega_X^{\ge p}(\log D)$ is also a finite filtration by subcomplexes. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 (Residues, signs and the Hodge shift.) For each ordered set $I$ of $a$ distinct components, write a term of $W_aL^k$ as $e_I\wedge\eta_I$ with $\eta_I$ regular, and restrict $\eta_I$ to $D_I$. These are separate residue coordinates on the separate summands of $D^{[a]}$. Terms with fewer poles restrict to zero in $\operatorname{Gr}^W_a$; a regular normal differential restricts to zero, and a coefficient vanishing on $D_I$ lies in the ideal generated by its normal coordinates, each factor $z_i$ converting $e_i$ to the regular form $dz_i$ and reducing the pole count. These observations prove that the kernel of the residue map on $W_a$ is exactly $W_{a-1}$. Conversely every regular stratum form extends locally in the normal coordinates and lifts as $e_I\wedge\eta_I$, proving surjectivity. Changes of local equations add only lower-pole terms, so these maps glue. The differential is $d(e_I\wedge\eta_I)=(-1)^a e_I\wedge d\eta_I$, agreeing with the differential of the shifted complex $[-a]$. Hence $\operatorname{Gr}^W_aL\cong i_{a*}\Omega_{D^{[a]}}^\bullet[-a]$, and $F^p$ corresponds to the stratum degree filtration $F^{p-a}$, the shift appropriate to a Tate twist $(-a)$. [F1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

2.2 (A pole-preserving local contraction.) Work on a smaller polydisc centered at a boundary point with $s$ normal coordinates. For tangential coordinates $w$, put $\phi_t(z,w)=(z,tw)$ and $R=\sum_jw_j\partial_{w_j}$. Set $h\eta=\int_0^1t^{-1}\phi_t^*(\iota_R\eta)\,dt$. Differentiating coefficients and basis differentials gives $\frac{d}{dt}\phi_t^*\eta=t^{-1}\phi_t^*(d\iota_R+\iota_Rd)\eta$; integration yields $dh+hd=\mathrm{id}-\phi_0^*$. The integrand has a finite limit at $t=0$ because contraction and pullback supply at least one tangential factor of $t$, and the power-series bounds of [F4] justify differentiation and integration on smaller polydiscs. This preserves every pole level, since it affects only regular tangential forms. What remains is the normal logarithmic complex with holomorphic coefficients $f(z)=\sum_{\nu\in\mathbb N^s}c_\nu z^\nu$ and differential $d(z^\nu e_I)=z^\nu(\sum_i\nu_i e_i)\wedge e_I$. For a nonzero multiindex $\nu$, choose the first index $i$ with $\nu_i>0$ and put $h_\nu=\nu_i^{-1}\iota_i$, contraction of the exterior algebra with the $i$-th basis vector. The identity $(\sum_j\nu_je_j)\wedge h_\nu+h_\nu(\sum_j\nu_je_j)\wedge=\mathrm{id}$ contracts that entire monomial summand. This also preserves $W$: in an $e_I$ monomial a logarithmic index with $\nu_i>0$ can be written as a regular differential by factoring $z_i$, so its effective pole count is precisely the number of indices $j\in I$ with $\nu_j=0$; $h_\nu$ removes only a positive-exponent index. Partitioning the series into the finitely many sectors specified by this first positive index and dividing coefficients by $\nu_i\ge1$ preserves normal convergence on each smaller polydisc, so these operators define a holomorphic homotopy. The single all-zero multiindex is left unchanged: its surviving complex is the exterior algebra on the $e_i$, with zero differential and $W_a$ equal to the span of wedges of degree at most $a$. This handles every pattern of simultaneous zero exponents and proves $\mathcal H^q(W_aL)_p=\bigwedge^q\mathbb C^s$ for $0\le q\le a$, and zero otherwise; inclusion $W_aL\to L$ induces the identity on these spaces. [F1, F4, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 (Every canonical truncation and the rational normalization.) Take the sheafification $\mathcal S_U^\bullet$ of smooth singular cochains on $U$. The flasque-resolution construction of [F6] applies to smooth simplices as well: barycentric subdivision and its prism operators preserve smoothness, local polydisc contractions are smooth, and the global small-simplex representative argument is unchanged. Thus $\mathcal S_U^\bullet$ resolves $\mathbb C_U$ and its terms are acyclic on every open subset. They are therefore $j_*$-acyclic, and $j_*\mathcal S_U^\bullet$ represents $Rj_*\mathbb C_U$. Integration of logarithmic forms on smooth simplices in $U$, with the cochain map and normalization of [F2], gives the chain map $L\to j_*\mathcal S_U^\bullet$. On the polydiscs of step 2.2 the target stalk cohomology is the cohomology of $(\Delta^*)^s\times\Delta^{d-s}$, the exterior algebra on meridians by [F4]. Integration gives $\int_{\gamma_i}e_j=2\pi i\delta_{ij}$, so the comparison is an isomorphism on every cohomology sheaf. Let $\tau_{\le a}$ denote the canonical truncation, with degree $a$ equal to the kernel of the next differential. Since every degree-$k$ logarithmic form has at most $k$ poles, the identity gives a genuine chain inclusion $\tau_{\le a}L\to W_aL$. By step 2.2 it induces an isomorphism in degrees at most $a$ and both sides have no cohomology above $a$, hence is a quasi-isomorphism for every $a$. These inclusions commute with the maps as $a$ increases. We therefore have the filtered comparison zigzag $(Rj_*\mathbb Q_U\otimes\mathbb C,\tau)\to(Rj_*\mathbb C_U,\tau)\leftarrow(L,\tau)\to(L,W)$, all arrows graded quasi-isomorphisms; exact scalar extension and the local finite torus cohomology establish the first arrow. On each graded sheaf the rational meridian wedge corresponds to $(2\pi i)^{-a}e_I$, which pairs by $1$ with the degree-$a$ meridian torus, not a degree-$2a$ class. Ordered residues thus identify $R^aj_*\mathbb Q_U$ with $i_{a*}\mathbb Q_{D^{[a]}}$ and place its comparison lattice in $(2\pi i)^{-a}\mathbb Q$, exactly the rational Tate normalization $(-a)$. [F2, F4, F6, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 (Actual filtered global-section models and a single comparison.) The sheaf comparison in step 3.1 is a zigzag, so it must not be treated as a nonexistent direct sheaf map in the opposite direction. Resolve the complexes and their filtrations by the exact Godement construction: $C^0(A)(V)=\prod_{x\in V}A_x$, with the natural embedding and successive cokernels. Stalks and products are exact for vector spaces under AC. Moreover $C^0(A)=\prod_{x\in X}i_{x*}A_x$ is an injective sheaf of field-vector spaces: each $A_x$ is injective over its field by extension of linear maps along a chosen complement, the exact stalk functor is left adjoint to $i_{x*}$, and a product of injectives is injective because the component extension maps can be chosen simultaneously under AC. The successive cokernel construction therefore gives an actual injective resolution. Exactness of $C^0$ and the short exact augmentation sequences give exactness of each successive cokernel functor by the snake lemma, so the resulting functorial resolution is exact on filtration levels, their finite intersections and both associated gradings; its global-section total computes derived global sections. Apply it to $L$ with $W,F$ and to the other weight-filtered models in the zigzag. Replace the rational and comparison models by $\tau_{\le d}$ first; their cohomology sheaves above $d$ vanish by the local torus calculation, so this is a quasi-isomorphism and leaves a finite weight range $0\le a\le d$. After resolution and global sections the complex-coefficient arrows in the zigzag are maps of weight-filtered vector-space complexes with graded quasi-isomorphisms. For the rational scalar-extension arrow, the global graded comparison is the isomorphism $H^{r-a}(D^{[a]};\mathbb Q)\otimes\mathbb C\to H^{r-a}(D^{[a]};\mathbb C)$ from [F3], with the normalization of step 3.1; this proves it is a graded quasi-isomorphism without interchanging tensor product with an infinite product of stalks. Such a map admits a weight-filtered homotopy inverse: its cone has acyclic weight-graded complexes; a cycle in $W_a$ has a leading graded preimage, and subtracting its differential lowers the cycle to $W_{a-1}$, so finite induction supplies a preimage in $W_a$. Thus the cone is acyclic with a $W$-strict differential. Choose filtration-compatible complements of its cycles and right inverses of its differential; the resulting degree-minus-one homotopy contracts the cone and preserves $W$, and the cone homotopy equations give a $W$-filtered homotopy inverse of the original map. AC permits these linear complements. Inverting the leftward comparison in step 3.1 and composing the remaining arrows gives an actual $W$-filtered chain map $K_{\mathbb Q}\otimes\mathbb C\to K_{\mathbb C}$, with $K_{\mathbb C}=\Gamma(X,C^\bullet(L))$ carrying the original $W,F$. Its graded maps are quasi-isomorphisms. Different inverse choices are filtered-homotopic, so their induced comparison and image filtrations on cohomology agree. These are bounded-below degreewise-finite filtered models of the type required in [F5]. [F6, A1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 (Strictness on the weight-graded global models.) Exactness of the resolution and step 2.1 identify $\operatorname{Gr}^W_aK_{\mathbb C}$ with a global-section resolution of $\Omega_{D^{[a]}}^\bullet[-a]$, with its degree Hodge filtration shifted by $a$. Its Hodge spectral sequence degenerates at $E_1$ by [F3]. This implies strictness of the differential of this actual filtered vector-space complex: if $dx$ belongs to $F^p$, take the leading $F$ index $b<p$ of $x$; its class in the associated-graded complex is a cycle. Degeneration means this $E_1$ class lifts to an actual cycle $y\in F^b$, up to an element of $F^{b+1}$ and a boundary in $F^b$. Subtract that cycle and boundary from $x$, preserving $dx$ and raising the filtration index of the preimage. Repeat through the finite filtration until a preimage of $dx$ lies in $F^p$. Thus $\operatorname{im}d\cap F^p=d(F^p)$. Moreover its degree-$r$ cohomology is $H^{r-a}(D^{[a]};\mathbb Q)(-a)$ under the comparison of step 3.1, with the induced $F$, pure of weight $r-a+2a=r+a$ and finite-dimensional by [F3]. Hence the global comparison models of step 4.1 satisfy every graded axiom of a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex, including strictness and the full induced Hodge filtration. [F3, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 (The mixed structure and its spectral sequence.) Apply the full conclusion of [F5] to the proved mixed Hodge complex of step 5.1. Its cohomology is $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ by steps 3.1-5.1 and [F6], and it carries the image Hodge filtration and shifted weight filtration $W_mH^n(U)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K))$. The weight spectral sequence is $E_1^{-a,q}=H^{q-2a}(D^{[a]};\mathbb Q)(-a)$, pure of weight $q$, degenerates at $E_2$, and gives $\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH^n(U)\cong E_2^{n-m,m}$ with its induced Hodge filtration. In particular this step uses the supplied recurrent-to-image-filtration proof, not an assumption that higher differentials preserve the desired filtration. [F5, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 (Lower weight bound and compactification image.) The pole index $a$ is nonnegative, so a term contributing to total degree $n=q-a$ has weight $q=n+a\ge n$. Hence step 6.1 gives $W_{n-1}H^n(U)=0$. Also $W_nH^n(U)$ is the image of $H^n(W_0K)$. On the complex side $W_0L=\Omega_X^\bullet$ by step 1.2; on the rational side $\tau_{\le0}Rj_*\mathbb Q_U=\mathbb Q_X$, since a punctured-coordinate polydisc is connected. Its map to $Rj_*\mathbb Q_U$ is restriction. Thus both sides identify $W_nH^n(U)$ with the actual image of $j^*:H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$, compatibly with the rational comparison and Hodge filtration. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.2, step 3.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 (Functoriality and independence.) A compactified extension $f:(X,D)\to(Y,E)$ of an open morphism satisfies $f^{-1}(E)\subseteq D$. A target boundary equation pulls back to a nonzero regular germ on each source component, since the dense open source maps into the target open. Its zero set is contained in $D$, so [F8] factors it locally as a unit times powers of source boundary equations with nonnegative integer exponents, so $f^*d\log t=d\log u+\sum_i m_i d\log z_i$. Wedges preserve pole count and degree, hence $f^*$ preserves $W,F$ on the logarithmic complexes and is compatible with the rational meridian comparison. The functorial resolutions and filtered comparison homotopies of step 4.1 produce the same natural pullback on cohomology; [F5] therefore makes it a mixed Hodge morphism. The graph-extension construction in [F7] supplies such compactified extensions after modifying the source. For two SNC compactifications of one $U$, a common SNC domination gives pullback comparison maps between their logarithmic mixed Hodge structures on $H^n(U)$, whose underlying rational maps are the identity. Strictness in [F5] makes these identity maps isomorphisms for both filtrations, proving independence. For any smooth projective compactification with arbitrary boundary, the modification-image clause of [F7] identifies its restriction image with the SNC one, so the formula of step 7.1 holds for it too. [F5, F7, F8, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra]

9.1 (Choice and boundary cases.) AC is inherited through the typed suppliers in [A1] and is also used exactly in step 4.1 for exact products in the Godement resolution and filtration-compatible vector-space complements to strictify the comparison zigzag. The monomial contractions, residues, rational meridian normalization, finite filtrations and weight bookkeeping are otherwise choice-free. With empty boundary $L=\Omega_X^\bullet$ and $W_0=L$, recovering the pure projective structure; empty $U$ may be represented by empty compactification and has zero cohomology, while the SNC compactification hypotheses already require density on every nonempty component. Components of differing dimensions are handled separately, empty strata vanish, and degrees outside the cohomological range give zero groups. This completes the retained full mixed Hodge, functoriality, independence, lower-weight and image claims. [A1, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra] ∎

items.statement: Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For $U=\mathbb C^\times\subset\mathbb P^1$, $H^1(U,\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q(-1)$, of weight $2$ and type $(1,1)$. In particular its weight is strictly larger than its cohomological degree.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; the smooth quasiprojective curve $U=\mathbb C^\times=\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)\setminus\{0,\infty\}$ with its SNC compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X=\mathbb P^1$, boundary $D=\{0\}\sqcup\{\infty\}$ ([[def-simple-normal-crossings-divisors]]).

[F1] The strata of the compactification. $D^{[0]}=X=\mathbb P^1$, $D^{[1]}=D$ is the disjoint union of the two points $0$ and $\infty$, and $D^{[a]}=\varnothing$ for $a\ge2$; all are smooth projective complex varieties of pure dimensions $1$ and $0$. The two projective coordinate charts identify the analytic space of $\mathbb P^1$ with the Riemann sphere, homeomorphic to $S^2$ by [[thm-stereographic-projection-riemann-sphere-homeomorphism]]. Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, [[thm-punctured-rn-deformation-retracts-onto-the-sphere]] gives the deformation retraction $H(z,t)=((1-t)+t/|z|)z$ onto $S^1$, so inclusion induces a homology isomorphism by [[prop-singular-homology-is-invariant-under-deformation-retracts]].

[F2] Cohomology of spheres ([[cor-homology-of-spheres]], [[cor-cohomology-over-a-field-is-dual-to-homology-over-that-field]]). Over $\mathbb Q$, $H_0(S^1)=H_1(S^1)=\mathbb Q$ and $H_n(S^1)=0$ otherwise, and the same pattern holds for $S^2$ in degrees $0$ and $2$; over the field $\mathbb Q$ evaluation identifies $H^n(-;\mathbb Q)$ with the full linear dual of $H_n(-;\mathbb Q)$. Hence $H^0(S^1;\mathbb Q)=H^1(S^1;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$ with higher groups zero, and $H^0(S^2;\mathbb Q)=H^2(S^2;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$ with $H^1(S^2;\mathbb Q)=0$; a point and a two-point space have cohomology $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb Q^2$ in degree $0$ and zero in positive degrees.

[F3] The logarithmic mixed Hodge structure ([[thm-logarithmic-complex-constructs-smooth-open-mixed-hodge-structures]]). For the SNC compactification of [F1] the logarithmic complex endows $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ with its weight filtration $W$, of weights at least $n$, satisfying $W_nH^n(U;\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))$, with weight spectral sequence $E_1^{-a,q}=H^{q-2a}(D^{[a]};\mathbb Q)(-a)\Rightarrow H^{q-a}(U;\mathbb Q)$ degenerating at $E_2$ and $\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH^n(U;\mathbb Q)\cong E_2^{n-m,m}$; the local residue normalization of that construction assigns to the closed logarithmic form $dz/z$ on $U$ the rational class $(2\pi i)^{-1}dz/z\in H^1(U;\mathbb Q)$, whose normalized rational residue coordinates at $0$ and at $\infty$ are $1$ and $-1$; the ordinary analytic residue of the normalized form is $(2\pi i)^{-1}$ times the corresponding coordinate.

[F4] Tate twist and type ([[def-rational-mixed-hodge-structure]]). The Tate structure $\mathbb Q(-1)$ is the pure rational Hodge structure of weight $2$ and type $(1,1)$, concentrated in $H^{1,1}$; a mixed Hodge structure whose weight-graded pieces are $\operatorname{Gr}^W_2=\mathbb Q(-1)$ and $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m=0$ for $m\ne2$ is pure of weight $2$ and type $(1,1)$.

[A1] AC is assumed and is consumed only through [F3] and its suppliers; the finite computations below are choice-free. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct: compute both sides of the weight spectral sequence of the logarithmic complex for $\mathbb P^1$ and identify the surviving degree-one term with the Tate twist.

1.1 The two cohomologies. By [F1] and [F2], $H^0(X;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$, $H^1(X;\mathbb Q)=0$, $H^2(X;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$; $H^0(D^{[1]};\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q^2$ and $H^1(D^{[1]};\mathbb Q)=0$; and $H^0(U;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$, $H^1(U;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$, $H^2(U;\mathbb Q)=0$, the generator being the meridian class dual to the circle. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The logarithmic generator. By the residue normalization of [F3] the class $(2\pi i)^{-1}dz/z$ is a nonzero rational class in $H^1(U;\mathbb Q)$ pairing by $1$ with the positively oriented meridian, so it generates the one-dimensional space $H^1(U;\mathbb Q)$ of step 1.1; its normalized rational residue coordinates at $0$ and $\infty$ are $1$ and $-1$, because in the coordinate $w=1/z$ at infinity the form $dz/z$ equals $-dw/w$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The weight spectral sequence. Only $a=0,1$ contribute. The $a=0$ column has $E_1^{0,0}=\mathbb Q(0)$, $E_1^{0,1}=0$, $E_1^{0,2}=H^2(\mathbb P^1;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q(-1)$, pure of weight $2$ and type $(1,1)$; the $a=1$ column has $E_1^{-1,2}=\mathbb Q(-1)^2$ and is otherwise zero. The sole possible nonzero differential is $d_1:E_1^{-1,2}\to E_1^{0,2}$, a pure Hodge morphism. Since the sequence degenerates at $E_2$ and $H^2(U)=0$ by step 1.1, its cokernel is zero, so its rank is one. The global closed logarithmic form of step 2.1 has normalized residue vector $(1,-1)$, which must survive this differential because it represents an actual cohomology class; hence this vector lies in its kernel. A rank-one map from a two-dimensional space has one-dimensional kernel, so $\ker d_1=\mathbb Q(1,-1)\cong\mathbb Q(-1)$. Equivalently, in a rational target generator normalized to the nonzero image of $(1,0)$, $d_1(r_0,r_\infty)=r_0+r_\infty$. Thus $E_2^{-1,2}=\mathbb Q(-1)$, $E_2^{0,2}=0$, $E_2^{0,0}=\mathbb Q(0)$, and all remaining terms vanish. This computes the required weight-graded piece without assuming an unproved Gysin normalization. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The mixed Hodge structure on $H^1(U,\mathbb Q)$. By [F3] the weight-graded piece $\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH^1(U;\mathbb Q)$ is $E_2^{1-m,m}$, so by step 3.1 it is $\mathbb Q(-1)$ for $m=2$ and vanishes for every other $m$; in particular $W_1H^1(U;\mathbb Q)=0$ and $W_2H^1(U;\mathbb Q)=H^1(U;\mathbb Q)$, which also agrees with the weights-at-least-$1$ and image formulas of [F3] and with $H^1(X;\mathbb Q)=0$ from step 1.1. By [F4] the class supported in weight $2$ with $\operatorname{Gr}^W_2=\mathbb Q(-1)$ makes $H^1(U;\mathbb Q)$ pure of weight $2$ and type $(1,1)$, so $H^1(U,\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q(-1)$; the classical generator $(2\pi i)^{-1}dz/z$ of step 2.1 is a rational class of this structure. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Conclusion and boundaries. The weight of $H^1(U,\mathbb Q)$ is $2$, strictly larger than the cohomological degree $1$, and the only nonzero Hodge number is $h^{1,1}=1$. The space $U$ is nonempty and disconnected cases do not arise; $H^0$ and $H^2$ of $U$ are handled by step 1.1 and carry weights $0$ and at most $2$; the two residue coordinates are the two components of $D$, and the kernel computation is finite linear algebra over $\mathbb Q$; no choice beyond [A1] is used. [A1, F4, step 2.1, step 4.1, given] ∎
